templates.name: Test pattern clip
templates.description: A colorful moving test pattern; works for any joke about waiting or glitching.

templates.name: Drake Hotline Bling
templates.description: Two-panel image of Drake: in the top panel he turns away with a disgusted hand-block gesture, in the bottom panel he points approvingly with a grin. Text sits to the right of each panel. Used to reject one option and endorse a better alternative — the classic 'this, not that' preference format.
example_captions: Spending 3 weeks on a rebrand nobody asked for
Actually emailing the 400 leads sitting in the CRM

templates.name: Two Buttons
templates.description: A sweating man in a red shirt agonizes over two large red buttons he must choose between, unable to press either. The two buttons carry conflicting options and the bottom label names the person paralyzed by the choice. Perfect for hypocrisy, impossible tradeoffs, and someone who clearly wants both.
example_captions: Cut ad spend to hit margin
Hit the aggressive Q4 growth target
Every marketing director in a board meeting
box_semantics: label for the sweating person facing the choice

templates.name: Distracted Boyfriend
templates.description: A man walking with his girlfriend turns around to ogle another woman passing by while his girlfriend glares at him in disgust. Three labels: the wandering man, the new temptation he's staring at, and the loyal partner he's neglecting. Used for abandoning something reliable in favor of a shiny new distraction.
example_captions: Startup founders
A brand-new AI tool with a waitlist
The email list that actually makes them money
box_semantics: the tempting new thing he's looking at
the loyal/existing thing being ignored (the girlfriend)

templates.name: Bernie I Am Once Again Asking For Your Support
templates.description: Bernie Sanders sits outdoors in a winter coat, gripping a folder, looking earnest and slightly weary as he makes a repeated plea. Top and bottom text frame the same tired request being made yet again. Used for anything you have asked for many, many times and still have not received.
example_captions: I am once again asking
for the client to send the brand assets they promised in March
box_semantics: the punchline of what is being asked for again

templates.name: UNO Draw 25 Cards
templates.description: A UNO player stares blankly at the camera while holding a fan of cards, faced with a choice between doing one simple thing or drawing 25 penalty cards. The joke is that they'd rather take the absurd punishment than do the easy thing. Great for stubbornness and refusal to change an obvious behavior.
example_captions: Write one subject line under 40 characters or draw 25
Our email copywriter, now holding 61 cards
box_semantics: the simple demand or challenge (or draw 25)
reaction/who refuses it — usually the drawn-25-cards punchline subject

templates.name: Left Exit 12 Off Ramp
templates.description: A car swerves violently across a highway divider at the last second to take Exit 12 instead of continuing straight. Labels go on the car (the person/entity), the sensible road ahead, and the exit they recklessly veer toward. Used for impulsive, self-destructive, or off-strategy decisions made at the last moment.
example_captions: Ship the roadmap we agreed on
Rebuild the whole homepage because a competitor changed theirs
Our CEO after one LinkedIn scroll
box_semantics: the exit being swerved toward (the tempting bad choice)

templates.name: Anakin Padme 4 Panel
templates.description: Four panels from Star Wars: Anakin states a plan, Padmé smiles and asks a hopeful clarifying question, Anakin stares back silently, and Padmé's smile drops into worry as she repeats the question. Used when someone's confident plan is missing a crucial part and the silence confirms the worst. The unanswered question is the whole joke.
example_captions: We're launching the campaign Monday
And we tested the checkout flow, right?
We tested the checkout flow, right?
box_semantics: the same question repeated with growing dread

templates.name: Always Has Been
templates.description: Two astronauts float above Earth; one points a gun at the other after a shocking realization, captioned with a naive question on top and the cold reply 'Always has been' below. Used to reveal that something was secretly true the whole time. Works for cynical truths and behind-the-curtain reveals.
example_captions: Wait, our whole growth strategy is just one guy posting on LinkedIn?
Always has been
box_semantics: the naive realization or question ('Wait, it's all X?')

templates.name: Epic Handshake
templates.description: Two muscular arms from Predator clasp in a triumphant handshake, each forearm labeled with a different party and the grip itself labeled with what they share. Used to point out an unexpected common ground between two very different groups. The joke lands hardest when the two labels are opposites.
example_captions: Interns on day one
20-year industry veterans
Googling what the acronym in the meeting meant
box_semantics: the thing they both do or agree on (the handshake)

templates.name: Sad Pablo Escobar
templates.description: Three panels of Pablo Escobar from the Narcos series sitting alone, looking around an empty space with increasing sadness and boredom. It conveys restless waiting, loneliness, and the slow dread of nothing happening. Best for dead pipelines, silent inboxes, and abandoned projects.
example_captions: Sent the proposal Tuesday
Followed up Thursday
Refreshing the inbox on Sunday night
box_semantics: the situation setup (what you're waiting on)

templates.name: Running Away Balloon
templates.description: A crying child desperately chases a floating balloon that has drifted out of reach, while an adult watches. Five labels cover the kid, the balloon, the hand that let go, the adult, and the surrounding context — a scene of something precious lost through carelessness. Used for grief over an opportunity, budget, or momentum that slipped away.
example_captions: The marketing team
The one post that finally went viral
Whoever deleted it for being 'off-brand'
The brand guidelines guy
Q3 engagement targets
box_semantics: the crying child chasing (who is upset)
the balloon floating away (what was lost)
the person/force that let it go
extra context or the background circumstance

templates.name: Gru's Plan
templates.description: Four panels of Gru presenting a plan on a flip chart: the first three boards show escalating steps, and in the fourth he stares in horror at the final board because the last step backfires on him. The fourth text box repeats the third — the reveal is that step three was the disaster. Perfect for plans with an unintended consequence you didn't think through.
example_captions: Discount the product 50% to spike signups
Signups triple overnight
Everyone churns the second the discount ends
Everyone churns the second the discount ends
box_semantics: same text as step three, now being stared at in horror

templates.name: Change My Mind
templates.description: Steven Crowder sits at a folding table on a campus lawn behind a banner stating a provocative opinion, with a sign reading 'Change My Mind'. The top text is usually a framing line and the banner carries the hot take. Used to state a bold or contrarian opinion and invite disagreement.
example_captions: Half of all 'strategy' meetings are just people reading a doc out loud
box_semantics: top framing line or setup (often left blank)
the bold opinion written on the banner

templates.name: Waiting Skeleton
templates.description: A skeleton sits slumped in a chair by a window, having clearly waited so long that it died there. Text above sets up what's being waited for and text below delivers the joke about the wait. Used for anything unbearably slow or never coming.
example_captions: Me waiting for legal to approve the tweet
It's 9 words long
box_semantics: the setup — what/who is being waited on
the punchline about how long the wait has been

templates.name: Marked Safe From
templates.description: A Facebook-style crisis-check banner with a profile photo and the phrase 'Marked Safe From', announcing survival of some ordeal. Used to joke about narrowly escaping a common annoyance or a widely dreaded event. The humor comes from applying disaster-level language to something trivial.
example_captions: Marked safe from
The 'quick sync' that was going to be an email
box_semantics: the header line, usually 'Marked safe from' plus the date/context
the trivial ordeal that was survived

templates.name: X, X Everywhere
templates.description: Buzz Lightyear holds Woody by the shoulder and gestures out at the horizon, saying 'X, X everywhere.' Both boxes name the same thing to convey overwhelming, inescapable abundance. Used when something is suddenly everywhere you look.
example_captions: AI-generated LinkedIn posts
AI-generated LinkedIn posts everywhere

templates.name: Disaster Girl
templates.description: A little girl smirks knowingly at the camera while a house burns down behind her and firefighters work the scene. Top text names the disaster and bottom text reveals her satisfied role in it. Used for gleeful, unbothered responsibility for chaos you caused.
example_captions: The whole team debugging the failed launch email
Me, who suggested 'let's just send it and see'
box_semantics: the disaster/scene unfolding in the background
the smug perpetrator's reaction or admission

templates.name: Trade Offer
templates.description: A bearded man in a red shirt announces 'I have a trade offer' with two panels beneath — what you receive on the left, what they receive on the right. Used for lopsided or absurd deals where one side clearly gets the better end. Great for negotiation and value-exchange jokes.
example_captions: I have a trade offer
You get: unlimited revisions
I get: paid in exposure
box_semantics: the header line ('I have a trade offer')

templates.name: Ancient Aliens
templates.description: Giorgio Tsoukalos from Ancient Aliens gestures emphatically with wild hair, mid-explanation, as the conspiracy-theorist expert. Text sets up a mundane phenomenon and the bottom line gives an unhinged explanation. Used for attributing something ordinary to a ridiculous cause with total conviction.
example_captions: I'm not saying the traffic spike was a bot farm
But the traffic spike was a bot farm
box_semantics: the setup — the phenomenon being explained

templates.name: Y'all Got Any More Of That
templates.description: A wide-eyed, disheveled man leans in desperately begging for more of a substance, in a scene played for addiction-craving humor. Top text names the thing being craved and bottom text is the desperate ask. Used for obsessive appetite — wanting more of something immediately and shamelessly.
example_captions: Me after one campaign hits 3x ROAS
Y'all got any more of that budget
box_semantics: setup naming who is craving or the context
the desperate ask — 'y'all got any more of that ___'

templates.name: Bernie Sanders Once Again Asking
templates.description: Bernie Sanders in mittens and a winter coat, seated with arms crossed at the inauguration, wearing an unimpressed expression while making yet another request. Top and bottom text carry the repeated, weary ask. Interchangeable with the other Bernie asking format — use for a demand you have made too many times.
example_captions: I am once again asking
everyone to actually fill in the CRM notes after their calls
box_semantics: the specific thing being asked for again

templates.name: Batman Slapping Robin
templates.description: A black-and-white comic panel of Batman slapping Robin mid-sentence, cutting him off hard. The top text is Robin's foolish statement and the bottom is Batman's corrective slap-line. Used to shut down a dumb take with blunt authority.
example_captions: Let's boost the post that already—
Boosting a bad post makes it a bad ad

templates.name: Mocking Spongebob
templates.description: SpongeBob hunched over in a chicken-like pose, used with alternating uppercase and lowercase text to mock someone by repeating what they said in a childish, sarcastic voice. The first box is the earnest statement and the second is the mocking echo. Used to ridicule a take you find absurd.
example_captions: We need to make the logo bigger
wE nEeD tO mAkE tHe LoGo BiGgEr
box_semantics: the original earnest statement being mocked
the same statement echoed in mocking sPoNgEbOb case

templates.name: Bike Fall
templates.description: Three panels of a cyclist who sticks a rod into his own front wheel, crashes, then lies on the ground blaming someone else. Labels go on the rider, the self-inflicted action, and the aftermath of blame. Used for self-sabotage followed by refusal to take responsibility.
example_captions: Our sales team
Ignoring every inbound lead for two weeks
Marketing isn't sending us any leads
box_semantics: the self-destructive action they take (stick in the wheel)
who or what they blame while lying on the ground

templates.name: Woman Yelling At Cat
templates.description: A split image: on the left a woman screams and points while crying at a dinner party; on the right a white cat sits at a dinner table looking smug and unbothered beside a salad plate. Used for a heated accusation met with total, infuriating calm. Great for irrational outrage versus a deadpan factual reply.
example_captions: THE WEBSITE REDESIGN TANKED OUR CONVERSIONS!!
you removed the pricing page

templates.name: One Does Not Simply
templates.description: A grim close-up of Boromir from Lord of the Rings raising one hand mid-speech, with text across the top and bottom. The format states that some task is deceptively hard — you cannot just walk in and do the obvious thing. Use it whenever a naive-sounding action turns out to be a nightmare in practice.
example_captions: One does not simply
get a one-line copy change approved by legal

templates.name: 0 days without (Lenny, Simpsons)
templates.description: Lenny from The Simpsons stands beside a workplace safety sign reading 'THIS FACTORY HAS GONE ___ DAYS WITHOUT AN ACCIDENT', with the counter reset to zero. The format tracks a recurring, entirely predictable failure that keeps happening. Use it for chronic mistakes, repeat offenders, and streaks that never last.
example_captions: days since a client asked if we can 'make the logo bigger'
box_semantics: the recurring incident that just happened again

templates.name: Is This A Pigeon
templates.description: A still from a dubbed anime where an android points at a butterfly and asks 'Is this a pigeon?' — confidently misidentifying something obvious. Labels go on the person, the butterfly, and the question caption. Use it when someone badly mislabels a thing while being totally sure of themselves.
example_captions: Founder
Posting once a month
Is this a content strategy?
box_semantics: the wrong label they're applying to it

templates.name: Mother Ignoring Kid Drowning In A Pool
templates.description: A mother in sunglasses lounges obliviously by a pool while a child flails and drowns behind her; a second figure looks on. Four labels mark the mother, the drowning kid, the pool, and the bystander. Use it when someone fixates on a trivial thing while a genuine crisis unfolds behind them, ignored.
example_captions: Leadership
Rebranding the deck
Churn up 40%
The whole support team
box_semantics: the thing they're absorbed in instead
the helpless observer who sees it

templates.name: Expanding Brain
templates.description: A four-panel stack of a human head with the brain glowing progressively brighter — from a small grey brain to a cosmic radiating galaxy-brain. Each row pairs with a caption that is supposedly more enlightened than the last, though the 'ascended' one is usually absurd. Use it for escalating takes, over-engineering, or ironic sophistication.
example_captions: Answering the client's email
Answering with a Loom video
Answering with a 40-slide strategy deck
Never answering and calling it 'creating scarcity'

templates.name: You Guys are Getting Paid
templates.description: SpongeBob and Patrick stare in shock as Squidward says the line — the format where someone discovers everyone else has been getting a benefit they never received. Two captions: the group's normal situation and the excluded person's stunned realization. Use it for being left out of a perk, a tool, or basic information.
example_captions: Everyone else has a documented onboarding process
You guys are getting onboarding?
box_semantics: the shocked reaction of the one who doesn't

templates.name: They're The Same Picture
templates.description: Pam from The Office holds up two nearly identical photos, asks the corporate trainer to spot the difference, and then insists 'they're the same picture.' Two labels for the pictures, one for the punchline. Use it when two things are presented as meaningfully different but are functionally identical.
example_captions: 'Growth hacking'
'Marketing'
They're the same picture
box_semantics: the punchline: they're the same picture

templates.name: Absolute Cinema
templates.description: A black-and-white shot of director Martin Scorsese with his hands raised toward his face in awe, captioned with the phrase 'Absolute Cinema.' The format sarcastically or sincerely declares something to be a masterpiece. Use it to crown a moment as peak art — whether it genuinely is, or is spectacularly mundane.
example_captions: Watching the client approve v1 with zero revisions
Absolute cinema
box_semantics: top caption: the subject or setup
bottom caption: usually 'Absolute cinema' or the awed verdict

templates.name: This Is Where I'd Put My Trophy If I Had One
templates.description: A man gestures proudly at a completely empty shelf, delivering the line about where he'd put his trophy if he had one. The format highlights an absence — an achievement, a resource, or a thing you conspicuously do not possess. Use it for self-deprecating jokes about lacking something everyone assumes you have.
example_captions: This is where I'd put my marketing budget
IF I HAD ONE

templates.name: Squidward window
templates.description: Squidward stares longingly out his window at SpongeBob and Patrick having fun without him, one hand on the sill. Text at the top and bottom frames who is watching and what they're watching. Use it for envy, exclusion, and the ache of watching others enjoy something you can't have.
example_captions: Me, still doing manual reporting
The team with an automated dashboard
box_semantics: who is looking in from outside
the enviable thing they're watching others do

templates.name: Megamind peeking
templates.description: Megamind peeks in from the edge of the frame with a smug, expectant look, usually paired with a taunting 'no ___?' question. The format mocks a conspicuous absence or calls out someone who came up empty. Use it for punchy callouts, missing deliverables, and gleeful gotchas.
example_captions: Sends the quarterly strategy deck
No numbers?

templates.name: Buff Doge vs. Cheems
templates.description: A split image: a muscular, heroic Shiba Inu (Buff Doge) on one side representing the strong past or ideal, and a small trembling Cheems on the other representing the weak present. Four text boxes label each dog and give each one a line. Use it for then-versus-now comparisons where one side is clearly superior.
example_captions: Agency in 2015
I'll cold call 200 people today
Agency in 2025
I can't send the email, it needs three approvals

templates.name: Tuxedo Winnie The Pooh
templates.description: A two-panel of Winnie the Pooh: plain Pooh on top for the ordinary version, and Pooh in a tuxedo on the bottom for the fancy, refined version of the same thing. The joke is that the classy phrasing means exactly the same as the plain one. Use it for pretentious rewording and upselling ordinary things.
example_captions: Guessing
Data-informed hypothesis testing
box_semantics: the fancy, elevated version of the same thing

templates.name: This Is Fine
templates.description: A cartoon dog in a hat sits calmly at a table sipping coffee while the entire room burns around him, saying 'This is fine.' Use it for denial in the middle of a disaster — a person or team insisting everything is under control while things collapse. Perfect for gallows humor about stress and dysfunction.
example_captions: Launch day, three critical bugs, CEO watching
This is fine
box_semantics: who is in denial / the burning situation

templates.name: Oprah You Get A
templates.description: Oprah Winfrey gestures wildly at her studio audience mid-giveaway, the classic 'YOU get a car!' moment. Two captions set up who is receiving and what they're all getting. Use it when something is being handed out indiscriminately to absolutely everyone.
example_captions: You get a 'Head of Growth' title
AND YOU GET A 'HEAD OF GROWTH' TITLE
box_semantics: who is receiving ('You get a X')

templates.name: Pawn Stars Best I Can Do
templates.description: Rick Harrison from Pawn Stars sits across the counter delivering his signature lowball: 'Best I can do is ___.' Top text is what's being offered or asked for; bottom is the insulting counteroffer. Use it for brutal negotiations, budget cuts, and comically low counters.
example_captions: Client wants a full brand refresh, website, and 6 months of content
Best I can do is $500 and exposure
box_semantics: what the other party wants or is offering

templates.name: Bell Curve
templates.description: A normal-distribution curve with three characters: a crying low-IQ wojak on the left, a smug midwit in the middle, and a serene robed sage on the right — the ends agreeing while the middle overcomplicates. Use it when the simplest answer and the most expert answer are the same, and only the mid-tier person insists on something elaborate.
example_captions: Just post consistently
Actually you need a multi-touch attribution model and a 12-persona matrix
Just post consistently

templates.name: Clown Applying Makeup
templates.description: A four-panel sequence of a man applying clown makeup step by step, ending in full clown face. Each caption is another self-deceiving justification, and by the last one it's obvious he's fooling himself. Use it for rationalizations that escalate into an obviously bad decision.
example_captions: They said the budget is tight but they love the work
They asked for a discount to 'start the relationship'
They want 4 free concepts to 'see the vision'
I'll do it, this could turn into a retainer
box_semantics: final line — full clown, the obvious truth

templates.name: where monkey
templates.description: A wide-eyed monkey in a cage looks around bewildered, captioned in broken English ('where monkey', 'where banana'). The format expresses confused searching for something that should obviously be there. Use it for dumb-but-relatable moments of looking for a missing thing.
example_captions: Opens the analytics dashboard after the tracking broke
where data

templates.name: Monkey Puppet
templates.description: The Japanese puppet monkey (Pedro) glances awkwardly to the side, then back — the face of someone who just realized they're implicated and hopes nobody noticed. Use it for guilty, awkward side-eye moments when you're quietly the cause of the problem being discussed.
example_captions: Manager: 'Who pushed to prod on Friday?'
*looks around nervously*

templates.name: I Bet He's Thinking About Other Women
templates.description: A couple lies in bed; the woman looks worried and thinks 'I bet he's thinking about other women,' while the man is actually thinking about something completely unrelated and mundane. Use it when someone assumes a deep or dramatic reason for silence and the real reason is trivial or absurd.
example_captions: I bet he's thinking about other women
Him: did I schedule that post for 9 AM or 9 PM
box_semantics: the worried assumption about what he's thinking

templates.name: Friendship ended
templates.description: The 'Friendship ended with MUDASIR, now SALMAN is my best friend' image — a photo collage with one friend crossed out and replaced by another. Use it for abruptly abandoning one tool, platform, habit, or ally in favor of a shiny replacement, with zero sentimentality.
example_captions: Friendship ended with SPREADSHEETS
Now NOTION is my best friend

templates.name: Soldier protecting sleeping child
templates.description: A weary soldier stands guard with a rifle while a small child sleeps peacefully behind him; a third label often marks the threat outside the frame. The format honors the unseen person absorbing the chaos so someone else can stay blissfully unaware. Use it for invisible labor and unsung protection.
example_captions: The ops person
The whole client-facing team
Three vendor invoices, a broken integration, and a payroll deadline
box_semantics: the protector doing the hard work

templates.name: They don't know
templates.description: A person stands alone at a party thinking a smug inner-monologue about the crowd: 'they don't know I ___.' The format captures imagined superiority over a room that is completely indifferent to you. Use it for niche pride, secret knowledge, or quietly cringe self-importance.
example_captions: At the networking mixer
they don't know my CTR went up 0.4% this week
box_semantics: the smug 'they don't know I ___' thought

templates.name: Spider Man Triple
templates.description: Three identical Spider-Men stand in a triangle pointing accusingly at each other — nobody can tell who's the real one, and each blames the others. Use it when several parties are indistinguishable, all pointing fingers, or when three supposedly different things are the same thing wearing different labels.
example_captions: Sales: marketing sent bad leads
Marketing: sales didn't follow up
Product: nobody told us what to build

templates.name: Hide the Pain Harold
templates.description: Elderly Hungarian stock-photo model Harold sits at a desk or holds a laptop, smiling faintly at the camera while his eyes betray quiet, resigned suffering. The format expresses false cheerfulness masking inner despair — saying something upbeat while the reality behind it is bleak. Use it for topics where someone performs contentment about a situation that is clearly going badly.
example_captions: "Wearing many hats" at a startup
I am the entire marketing department

templates.name: All My Homies Hate
templates.description: A rough hand-drawn scribble of a cowboy at a campfire with a speech bubble, in crude MS Paint style. The top text names a thing you hate, and the second line repeats it in the format "all my homies hate X" — expressing unanimous, tribal, no-debate disdain shared by you and your whole crew. Use it for universally loathed tools, practices, or people in a given community.
example_captions: I hate "quick sync to align"
All my homies hate "quick sync to align"
box_semantics: group echo confirming everyone hates it too

templates.name: Two guys on a bus
templates.description: Two men sit on opposite sides of a bus: one stares out at a bleak gray view looking miserable, the other looks out at a beautiful sunny landscape looking blissful. Same bus, same trip, radically different experience based on perspective or one small choice. Use it for comparing two people facing the same situation where one setup or mindset makes it pleasant and the other makes it torture.
example_captions: Manually pulling numbers for the weekly report
Automated dashboard that emails itself
box_semantics: the miserable version of the situation
the blissful version of the same situation

templates.name: Imagination Spongebob
templates.description: SpongeBob SquarePants holds up his hands framing a rainbow with the word "imagination," grinning with sarcastic wonder. The format mocks magical thinking — presenting a lazy, hand-wavy, or delusional solution as if it were visionary. Use it when someone skips the hard part and gestures vaguely at a miracle.
example_captions: How are we hitting 10x revenue with no ad budget?
Going viral
box_semantics: the magic word that supposedly makes it work

templates.name: Roll Safe Think About It
templates.description: A young man in a suit taps his temple with a knowing smirk, as if he has just outsmarted everyone. The format delivers fake-clever "logic" — advice that sounds like a life hack but is actually absurd or self-defeating. Use it for cursed shortcuts and technically-true reasoning that solves a problem by ignoring it.
example_captions: Can't have a bad churn rate
if you never onboard any customers

templates.name: Boardroom Meeting Suggestion
templates.description: A four-panel cartoon of a boardroom where an executive asks for ideas, two people give bland answers, and a third makes an honest suggestion — and is thrown out the window. The format expresses the punishment of blunt truth in a corporate setting where only safe, useless answers are welcome. Use it for topics about honesty being unwelcome, obvious solutions being ignored, or institutional denial.
example_captions: How do we improve customer retention?
Loyalty points!
A new brand color!
Fix the product
box_semantics: the honest suggestion that gets you defenestrated

templates.name: Sleeping Shaq
templates.description: A split image of Shaquille O'Neal: on top he's slumped asleep, indifferent, and below he's suddenly awake, alert, and energized. The format contrasts something that should matter but gets zero reaction with something trivial that grabs total attention. Use it for misplaced priorities and selective enthusiasm.
example_captions: Quarterly revenue down 30%
Someone changed the logo without asking
box_semantics: the thing that instantly gets everyone's attention

templates.name: Flex Tape
templates.description: Infomercial pitchman Phil Swift holds a roll of Flex Tape and slaps it over a massive leak, followed by the boat being sawed in half and taped back together. The format expresses a comically inadequate quick fix slapped onto a catastrophic problem. Use it for band-aid solutions, hacks in production, and patching over structural failure.
example_captions: Entire funnel broken before the launch
A discount code
Marketing at 4:55pm on Friday
box_semantics: the person or team doing the patching

templates.name: Three-headed Dragon
templates.description: King Ghidorah, a three-headed golden dragon, where each head is labeled — two heads look identical and menacing while the third is comically goofy or weak. The format sets up a trio that should be equally powerful but where one member is obviously the weak link. Use it for teams, tech stacks, or trios where one element is embarrassingly out of place.
example_captions: Our growth engine
SEO
Paid ads
Terrance posting on LinkedIn

templates.name: George Bush 9/11
templates.description: President George W. Bush sits in a classroom chair reading with children as an aide leans in to whisper the news to him; his face stays blank. The format captures the moment devastating news is delivered to someone mid-activity, and their reaction is delayed, frozen, or absent. Use it for the exact instant a disaster lands during something trivial.
example_captions: Me presenting our flawless launch plan to the client
"The payment processor just went down"
box_semantics: what the person is doing / the mundane setting

templates.name: Inhaling Seagull
templates.description: A seagull inhales dramatically with its beak wide open before screaming, shown across escalating panels. The format expresses an inevitable, exhausted, over-the-top outburst about to erupt — usually after a long buildup of small annoyances. Use it for the moment restraint finally breaks.
example_captions: Client approves the final design
"Can we see it in a different font?"
*inhales*
WE ARE THREE ROUNDS PAST FINAL

templates.name: Megamind no bitches
templates.description: Megamind's blue head presses against the glass with the caption "no bitches?" — a smug, mocking interrogation of someone's obvious lack of something. The format delivers a deadpan roast in the form of a rhetorical question about a glaring absence. Use it for calling out missing results, missing users, or missing credibility.
example_captions: Six months of content strategy
No customers?
box_semantics: the setup / the boast being deflated
the mocking question about what's missing

templates.name: Types of Headaches meme
templates.description: A medical-style diagram showing several head silhouettes with different pain regions labeled by headache type, ending with one final panel showing the whole head shaded in for the worst kind. The format ranks ordinary irritations against one supreme, all-consuming source of pain. Use it for declaring what truly causes maximum suffering in a category.
example_captions: Tension headache, migraine, cluster headache
"Just make the logo bigger" headache

templates.name: No - Yes
templates.description: A two-panel image where a figure firmly refuses something in the top panel and then eagerly accepts something nearly identical in the bottom panel. The format expresses inconsistent standards — rejecting a thing on principle, then embracing the same thing when it's framed differently. Use it for hypocrisy, rebranding, and selective enthusiasm.
example_captions: "Cold email"
"Personalized outbound sequence"

templates.name: Panik Kalm Panik
templates.description: Three panels of the Meme Man face: alarmed "PANIK," relieved "KALM," then alarmed "PANIK" again. The format tracks an emotional rollercoaster where a scare is briefly resolved and then immediately made worse by a follow-up realization. Use it for any three-beat setup → relief → deeper problem.
example_captions: The campaign got zero conversions
It was just a broken tracking pixel
The pixel has been broken since January

example_captions: Client seeing the invoice, then seeing the rush fee line item under it

templates.name: Brad Pitt eating
templates.description: Brad Pitt calmly eating on camera, unbothered while something happens elsewhere. The go-to for spectating chaos you're not responsible for — competitor meltdowns, comment-section wars, or watching a decision you warned about play out.
example_captions: Us reading the reviews of the competitor who said our category was 'basically dead'

templates.name: Sabalenka’s reaction to the point by Fernandez
templates.description: A pro tennis player frozen at the net, watching a shot she can't do anything about. Use it for the moment a rival pulls off something genuinely good — grudging respect, getting outplayed, or realizing you just got beaten on your own turf.

templates.name: Ryan Gosling Blade Runner sad edit
templates.description: A lone figure hunched on snowy steps as the weather buries him — pure cinematic defeat. Built for quiet burnout: the aftermath of a failed launch, a dead campaign, or realizing the work meant nothing to anyone but you.
example_captions: Me after six weeks on the rebrand, watching the founder ask if we can 'just go back to the old logo'

templates.name: i am spiderman
templates.description: Tobey Maguire on the phone, quietly owning up to who he actually is. Use it for the reveal — admitting you're the one behind the account, the culprit of the outage, or the person who has to fix this because nobody else can.
example_captions: Client: 'whoever runs your TikTok is a genius' — me, who runs the TikTok, on the call

templates.name: some sort of comp
templates.description: A blindfolded kid swinging at a target he can't see, surrounded by people watching. The format for confident action with zero visibility — guessing at strategy, targeting without data, or flailing at a goal while stakeholders spectate.

templates.name: Robert Pattinson Walking With The Boys
templates.description: Two men in sharp suits striding somewhere with total conviction while things blow up behind them. Squad energy — the team walking in to take over, a coordinated launch, or showing up somewhere you weren't invited and owning it.
example_captions: Agency walking into the account that fired three vendors before us

templates.name: Walter White taking out cash from washing machine
templates.description: Walter White hauling stacks of cash out of a washing machine. Use it for money showing up from somewhere nobody expected — a sleeper channel, an old asset that suddenly prints, or a revenue line you forgot you had.
example_captions: Checking the abandoned-cart email nobody's touched since 2023 and finding it did $60k this quarter

templates.name: tank
templates.description: First-person view from inside a tank, rolling forward with everything in front of it. For overwhelming force applied to a modest problem — a huge budget, a full team, or an enterprise tool aimed at something tiny.

templates.name: cat vibing
templates.description: Nyan Cat looping on a laptop screen, rainbow trail and all — pure oblivious vibes. Use it for happily ignoring the problem, coasting while the dashboard burns, or the one calm thing in a bad week.

templates.name: Joe Goldberg template
templates.description: Joe Goldberg staring hard at someone who doesn't know they're being studied. The template for unsettling levels of attention — deep lead research, stalking a competitor's every post, or knowing far too much about your ICP.

templates.name: cat
templates.description: A hand pushing a charger into a wall outlet — simple, satisfying, decisive. Use it for plugging something in: a new integration, a fresh budget into a channel that works, or finally connecting the two tools that should've talked months ago.

templates.name: d2c2

templates.name: hector
templates.description: Hector Salamanca glaring upward with total fury and no way to express it. The format for silent, immobilized rage — reading feedback you can't argue with, sitting in a meeting you were overruled in, or watching a bad idea get approved.

templates.name: Avengers getting ready

templates.name: Jake Gyllenhaal doing research

templates.name: Berserk template

templates.name: Ryan Gosling Emma Stone La La Land

templates.name: Sad compilation

templates.name: Thanos sad

templates.name: Pam "They're the Same Picture" Papers
templates.description: Pam holds up two sheets that are obviously identical while insisting she sees a difference — the format for calling out fake distinctions. Reach for it when a competitor, a rebrand, or a 'new' feature is functionally the same thing with a different label.
example_captions: Our 2024 brand refresh
Our 2025 brand refresh

templates.name: Thanos "They Called Me a Mad Man"
templates.description: Thanos surveys the wreckage and reminds everyone he was doubted before he was right. Use it for vindication posts — the unpopular bet, the channel nobody believed in, the call your team pushed back on that just printed.
example_captions: They called me a mad man for putting the whole Q3 budget into a niche newsletter with 4,000 subscribers

templates.name: Master Oogway "There Are No Accidents."
templates.description: Oogway delivers a calm, cosmic truth that lands heavier than it should. Good for framing a 'coincidence' as an inevitable outcome — when a result was clearly caused by the thing you've been telling everyone to do.
example_captions: "Our best month came right after we finally fixed onboarding"
There are no accidents.

templates.name: This Is Not Fine
templates.description: The dog-in-a-burning-room bit, but the mask is off — everything is on fire and the subject openly admits it's bad. Use it when the situation has passed the point of coping humor and you're naming the disaster out loud.
example_captions: Ad account disabled, retainer client ghosting, and the site went down — all before the 9am standup

templates.name: Third Place Celebration - Bronze Medal
templates.description: A guy gets bronze, sulks for a second, then escalates into a full gold-medal celebration. It's the format for taking a modest or third-place result and hyping it anyway — perfect for small wins you're choosing to be loud about.
example_captions: Ranked #3 for our main keyword
Wait, that's page one
BEST IN THE INDUSTRY (per our new landing page)

templates.name: Tintin "Yes, They're Absolutely Identical"
templates.description: Tintin holds two things side by side and confirms with total certainty that they're the same. Same job as any 'no difference' format, but with a smug, matter-of-fact tone — best when *you're* the one pointing out the redundancy, not the one being fooled.
example_captions: The $2,000/mo enterprise plan
The $49/mo plan with a different logo

templates.name: Two Characters Survival Water
templates.description: One character calmly explains a survival fundamental while the other sobs and drinks anyway — knowing the rule and following it are different things. Use it when someone is being lectured on the very thing they're already failing at, in real time.
example_captions: You have to post consistently to grow
I know
Consistency is the whole game
I know
*posts once a month, cries about reach*

templates.name: Scared Tom Cat
templates.description: Tom's face frozen mid-horror — the reaction shot for information you cannot unsee. Best for the moment a number, a bill, or a client message lands and the whole body reacts before the brain does.
example_captions: Opening the ad spend dashboard on the 1st of the month
Realizing the campaign ran all weekend with no cap

templates.name: Disturbed Tom Redraw
templates.description: A cleaner, more unsettling redraw of the horrified Tom face — the same shock, dialed up and lingering longer. Use it when the thing you saw wasn't just surprising but genuinely disturbing to think about.
example_captions: Doing a content audit on the posts from before we hired a copywriter
There are 47 of them

templates.name: Swole Tom and Small Jerry
templates.description: A hulking Tom looms over a tiny, terrified Jerry — pure power imbalance. Reach for it whenever one side massively outmatches the other: budget, distribution, headcount, or leverage in a negotiation.
example_captions: Their $4M brand campaign
Our founder posting from his personal account

templates.name: Tom and Jerry: Backfired Shotgun
templates.description: Tom aims at Jerry and blows himself up instead — the anatomy of a self-inflicted wound. Use it for tactics that backfire directly onto the person who launched them.
example_captions: Us, sending an aggressive competitor-comparison email blast
Us, watching them retweet it to 200k followers

templates.name: Grant Gustin Peace Sign by Grave
templates.description: A guy in a suit throws a peace sign next to a fresh grave — cheerful closure over something that just died. Perfect for killing a project, sunsetting a feature, or ending a process nobody will miss.
example_captions: Me after finally cancelling the tool stack nobody logged into
RIP six SaaS subscriptions, $1,400/mo

templates.name: French Government Funeral
templates.description: A row of officials grinning and posing at a graveside — the collective, unbothered burial. Use it when a whole team or org cheerfully signs off on the end of something, with zero mourning.
example_captions: The entire leadership team after the vote
Here lies the weekly all-hands, 2019–2025

templates.name: Toucan Face Swap
templates.description: A human face grafted onto a toucan — something uncanny that's trying very hard to pass as normal. Use it for output that's technically on-brand but deeply, visibly wrong.
example_captions: Client: "just make it look like our brand but fresher"
The eighth revision

templates.name: Trade Offer I Receive, You Receive
templates.description: A mock deal sheet splitting what each side gets, built so the two columns are wildly lopsided. Reach for it any time you're exposing a bad bargain — pricing, contracts, unpaid 'exposure' offers, or what a tool actually gives back for the money.
example_captions: Enterprise SaaS sends a trade offer
Your card charged every month until the heat death of the universe
Two seats and a Slack channel nobody opens

templates.name: Trust Nobody Not Even Yourself
templates.description: A formal I-receive / you-receive exchange laid out with a straight face, usually wildly lopsided. Built for pitching a deal, an offer, or a swap — either a genuinely good one or a comically bad one.
example_captions: Trade offer
I receive: your email address
You receive: the 40-page playbook we charged $300 for last year

templates.name: Hood Documentary Roll Safe - Eddie Murphy Thinking
templates.description: Someone gets ambushed by a copy of themselves — the enemy is in the mirror. Use it for self-sabotage: the process you built that now blocks you, or the past decision that's currently ruining your week.
example_captions: Me, trying to ship the new landing page
Me from six months ago, who built the CMS "temporarily"

templates.name: Triangle Jerry
templates.description: The finger-to-temple genius pose, used for logic that's clever right up until you think about it. Best for shortcut reasoning that solves a metric while quietly ignoring the actual goal.
example_captions: Can't have a high bounce rate
if nobody visits the site
Can't miss your CAC target
if you don't run any ads
Zero churn if you have zero customers

templates.name: Triangle Jerry and Cube Tom
templates.description: Jerry, redrawn as a smug little triangle, radiating unearned contentment. Use it for the small, dumb, deeply satisfying win — the thing that shouldn't have worked but did.
example_captions: Spent three weeks on the funnel rebuild
The 'reply YES' post outperformed it

templates.name: Soyjaks Pointing
templates.description: Tom and Jerry redrawn as blunt geometric shapes — two entities reduced to their crudest possible form. Good for stripping a complicated-sounding comparison down to what it actually is.
example_captions: Our 47-slide growth strategy deck
"Post more, charge more"

templates.name: Two Perspectives on a Bus
templates.description: Two identical figures pointing and gasping at the same thing — mutual, excited recognition. Use it for the moment two parties discover they're doing the exact same thing, or for calling out a shared obvious truth.
example_captions: Our agency pitching "AI-powered growth"
The 400 other agencies pitching "AI-powered growth"

templates.name: Unsheathing Sword
templates.description: Two men on the same bus, one facing bleak rocks and one facing sunlit mountains — identical situation, opposite outlook. Use it for framing: same data, same quarter, same feedback, two completely different reads.
example_captions: "Only 12 people signed up" vs "12 people we can call personally this week"

templates.name: Kamina's Sword Unsheathed
templates.description: Hands drawing a blade against open sky — the pre-fight moment, right before someone commits. Use it for the escalation point: the reply-all you're about to send, the competitor you're about to name, the price you're about to raise.
example_captions: Client says the deliverable "just needs one small tweak" for the fifth time
Opening the scope-of-work document

templates.name: Understandable Have A Great Day
templates.description: Two cars passing in opposite directions — one driver horrified, the other grinning like a menace. Use it for the split second where two parties pass each other with completely different energy, usually right before one of them finds out.
example_captions: Me leaving Friday's launch review, exhausted
The intern who just got publishing access, driving toward the content calendar

templates.name: Uno Reverse Water
templates.description: A muscular guy reaches out while another walks away from him — the classic virgin/chad walk-off, used to score two approaches against each other. Reach for it when contrasting the confident, simple move with the anxious, over-engineered one.
example_captions: Guy who A/B tested the button color for six weeks
Guy who just shipped it and asked customers

templates.name: Kamina Sword Unsheathed
templates.description: A two-beat unsheathe — grip, then full blade revealed. The build-and-reveal version of the escalation format: setup on top, the thing you're actually bringing on the bottom.
example_captions: "Can you show us why your retainer is worth it?"
*pulls up the 14-month attribution report*

templates.name: Kamina's Sword Unsheathed 2
templates.description: Shaq gives a peace sign with a flat, unbothered 'understandable, have a great day' — total non-resistance. Use it for the rejection, objection, or bad news you're choosing not to fight about.
example_captions: Sent a cold pitch, spent two hours on it
Reply: "not interested, remove me"
Understandable, have a great day

templates.name: Forehead Vein
templates.description: An Uno reverse card held up to running water, physically bending the stream backwards — the impossible counter. Use it when something gets turned straight back on the sender: an objection, a criticism, a competitor's own tactic.
example_captions: Competitor runs ads on our brand name
We bid on theirs and got a 3x lower CPC

templates.name: Elliot Page Driving Past Pink Guy
templates.description: A blade that keeps extending across panels, longer each time — escalation with no ceiling. Use it when a small ask, a small fix, or a small campaign keeps growing well past its original size.
example_captions: "Quick landing page refresh"
Now includes a rebrand, a new CMS, and a podcast

templates.name: Virgin vs. Chad Walking
templates.description: The same face twice — once with the stress vein bulging, once calm. A direct before/after for pressure: what a task does to you versus what it does to you once something changed.
example_captions: Building the monthly client report by hand
Building it after we templated the whole thing

templates.name: Volleyball Player Booty
templates.description: A close-crop sports shot that lands as pure attention bait — two nearly identical options presented for inspection. Reach for it when the joke is that a buyer can't tell two things apart, or when the visual is doing the clicking and the text is doing the selling.
example_captions: The agency that charges $12k/mo
The agency that white-labels the same $400 freelancer

templates.name: Virgin vs Chad Girl
templates.description: The classic two-column status format: a hunched, over-explaining figure on the left, a serene confident one on the right. Use it to make one approach look cowardly and overthought while the other looks obvious and correct — great for calling out process theater versus just shipping.
example_captions: Runs it past legal, brand, and three stakeholders before posting
Posts it

templates.name: Volume up Crying Guy
templates.description: Six escalating beats of someone sobbing into their headphones while cranking the dial louder anyway. Built for a spiral — a bad number or a brutal truth that gets worse each line while the subject keeps voluntarily consuming it.
example_captions: opens the analytics dashboard
traffic down 40%
scrolls further
it's down 40% on the page we spent Q3 rebuilding
keeps scrolling
the one blog post from 2019 is still the #1 driver

templates.name: Men's Room Urinal Etiquette
templates.description: A restroom lineup gag about proximity and unspoken rules — who parks right next to you when there was clearly space. Use it for boundary violations, uninvited closeness, and competitors or coworkers who crowd your lane for no reason.
example_captions: Me, posting in a niche with four total accounts
The brand that launched an identical account 48 hours later

templates.name: Thanos What Did It Cost? Everything.
templates.description: The Infinity War exchange where a hard-won result is priced out in one word: everything. Deploy it when a win came at absurd cost — the launch shipped, the deal closed, and something else quietly died to make it happen.
example_captions: "So you finally hit the Q4 revenue target?"
"Yes." / "What did it cost?" / "The entire content team."

templates.name: What Did It Cost Thanos
templates.description: Quieter cut of the Gamora-and-Thanos confrontation, weighted toward the aftermath rather than the punchline. Best for retrospectives — the thing you gave up months ago to get where you are now, stated flatly.
example_captions: "You really did rank #1 for the keyword."
"It took every drop of the brand voice to get there."

templates.name: Bugs Bunny Holding Back
templates.description: One character physically restraining another mid-lunge. The format for intervention — stopping someone right before they do the impulsive, expensive thing, or admitting you're the one who needs holding back.
example_captions: Client, three days into a rebrand: "Let's also change the domain"
Me, holding the strategy doc like a leash

templates.name: Spongebob Judging Fish
templates.description: A fish clutching a drink and radiating silent, total judgment. Use it for the deadpan side-eye — reacting to a claim, a pitch deck, or a metric that everyone in the room knows is nonsense.
example_captions: "We're pre-revenue but the TAM is $40 billion"
The one person in the room who's read the churn report

templates.name: Zac Efron Explaining
templates.description: Zac Efron mid-gesture, animatedly explaining something with total sincerity and zero self-awareness. Reach for it when someone earnestly presents an idea that is obviously, visibly bad to everyone else — the confident wrong answer.

"People will just find us organically"

templates.name: Void Cat Blep
templates.description: A black cat composed and dignified in the first frame, tongue out and unhinged in the second. The before/after of a facade slipping — the polished version versus the one that appears the second the meeting ends.

My tone in the internal Slack thread 90 seconds later

templates.name: What If I Told You
templates.description: Morpheus mid-revelation, sunglasses reflecting the person about to have their worldview adjusted. One text box, one uncomfortable truth — ideal for reframing something the audience assumed was settled.

templates.name: Whispering Ear Cringe
templates.description: One person whispers something at a party, the other recoils in open disgust. Built for the reveal-and-reaction pair — say the quiet thing in box one, let the face do the review in box two.

The ops lead who has to reconcile it

templates.name: Will Smith Slaps Chris Rock at the Oscars
templates.description: A live-TV slap: a joke lands, retaliation arrives instantly. Use it for immediate, disproportionate consequence — poking something you shouldn't have, and the response arriving before you finish the sentence.

The project manager

templates.name: Steve Harvey Shocked
templates.description: Steve Harvey stunned behind a multiple-choice board, unable to process the options in front of him. Use it when every available answer is somehow wrong, or when the correct one is so grim it needs a host reacting to it.
example_captions: Where does your marketing budget actually go?
A: Ads nobody clicks
B: A tool nobody logs into
C: The retainer nobody audits

templates.name: Steve Harvey Two Zero Two Four
templates.description: The expanded quiz-board version of Harvey's shocked reaction, with room for a question and a full slate of increasingly damning options. Best for long, layered jokes where the humor builds across the answer list.

A
The creative was recycled
B
The landing page 404'd
C
It launched on a holiday
D
All of it, simultaneously, on purpose

templates.name: Will Smith Four Panel
templates.description: Will Smith in a suit cycling through expressions against a carnival backdrop — the shape of an opinion changing in real time. Use it for the before-and-after of a mind being changed, usually by data nobody wanted to see.
example_captions: Me defending the brand-awareness campaign
Me reading that it drove eleven visits and two of them were mine

templates.name: Task Failed Successfully
templates.description: A vintage Windows error box announcing that the task failed successfully. The go-to for technically-shipped-but-actually-broken — three boxes for title, message, and the button you have no choice but to click.

Ad approved, budget spent, zero impressions delivered
OK

templates.name: Winnie the Pooh Reading
templates.description: Pooh squinting at a page with visible confusion and mild revulsion. Best for reacting to a document — a brief, a contract, an analytics export — that makes less sense the longer you look at it.

Fourteen pages, no target audience, one hex code

templates.name: Cursed Winnie the Pooh
templates.description: Pooh with a too-wide, too-many-teeth grin that reads as a threat. Use it for forced enthusiasm — the smile you hold while agreeing to something that will ruin your week.

Me: "Of course!"

templates.name: Winnie the Pooh Discerning
templates.description: Two-panel Pooh: casual on top, refined and faintly superior on the bottom. The standard upgrade format — same idea, fancier framing, and the fancy version is the flex.

Initiating a multi-touch nurture sequence

templates.name: Wojak Crying Hug
templates.description: One Wojak sobbing while another holds them. Use it for solidarity in a shared miserable experience — the moment somebody finally admits the thing everyone was quietly enduring.

"They always do"

templates.name: Red vs. Blue Gang Members
templates.description: Two stylized figures in opposing red and blue colors, ready to fight over territory. Reach for it when a rivalry is loud but the underlying thing is identical — tool wars, platform tribes, and factions arguing over cosmetics.

Team "post daily on X"

templates.name: Good Burger "Wooo!" Laser Eyes
templates.description: Glowing red eyes and lens flare — hype at maximum voltage. Use it for the moment something clicks and restraint leaves the building: a number spikes, an idea lands, and now you're unstoppable.

"Turn the budget up"

templates.name: Woman Yelling At Cat

The freelancer, replying with a thumbs up

templates.name: Woody Fighting Himself

Me adding four more sections to it

templates.name: Woman Yelling at Cat
templates.description: Blank yelling-woman-and-cat layout with room for a fuller setup on each side. Same accuser-versus-unmoved dynamic, but sized for longer text — good when the complaint needs actual specifics.

Leadership, asking for the ROI breakdown by channel

templates.name: SpongeBob SquarePants Patrick Reveals Insides
templates.description: A setup panel followed by an unflattering look at what's actually inside. Use it for the teardown — the polished offer in frame one, the ugly mechanics holding it together in frame two.

Four Zapier steps and a Google Sheet

templates.name: Two Girls Comparing Boobs
templates.description: A side-by-side of two figures at visibly different scales — the format for a size or magnitude comparison. Use it when the joke is that one number, budget, or audience dwarfs the other and everyone can see it.

Their conversion rate

templates.name: Yes Chad
templates.description: The stoic profile of a man who is simply not going to argue with you. One box, one unbothered stance — perfect for owning a take other people find embarrassing.

templates.name: Wait, You Guys Are Getting Paid?

templates.name: We're the Millers You Guys Are Getting Paid

Wait — we're getting paid to post memes?

templates.name: Yes Chads Kissing
templates.description: Two confident 'Yes Chad' profiles turn toward each other and lock lips — the format for two things that were supposed to be rivals discovering they're a perfect match. Use it for surprise alignment: two tools, two teams, or two strategies that turn out to love each other.

Marketing team
Both realizing the lead-scoring model actually works

templates.name: Avengers: Endgame "You Took Everything From Me, I Don't Even Know Who You Are"

Them, who have never once heard our name

templates.name: You're Weak. I'm You.

The undocumented script you shipped in March

templates.name: Obi-Wan Kenobi 'You Were Supposed to Destroy Them, Not Join Them'

templates.name: Perry the Platypus "Every Day. We Stray Further from God."

Adding AI to the AI that manages the AI

templates.name: Shrek Good Question
templates.description: A knowing smirk aimed straight at the viewer — the reaction to a question that lands harder than the asker realized. Use it for the awkward metric, the pricing question, or the thing your team quietly avoids answering.

templates.name: Titanic "He Exists Now. Only in My Memory."
templates.description: Wistful, elegiac reflection on something that only survives in memory now. Built for sunsetted features, dead channels, cheap ad rates, and anything the market quietly killed.

templates.name: Ew, I Stepped in Shit
templates.description: Instant disgust followed by the close-up confirmation of exactly what you stepped in. Use it for the two-beat reveal: something feels off, then you look and it's worse than you thought.

47 active campaigns, none of them tagged

templates.name: Kung Fu Panda "Finally! A Worthy Opponent!"

The client who reads every line of the analytics report

templates.name: Is It Possible to Learn This Power?
templates.description: Wide-eyed, slightly desperate interest in a skill someone else clearly has. Use it for envy of a competitor's move, a coworker's superpower, or any trick you'd very much like taught to you.

templates.name: Mickey Mouse Clubhouse "It's a Surprise Tool That Will Help Us Later"

templates.name: Dio Brando "I've Seen Enough. I'm Satisfied."
templates.description: Cold, immediate satisfaction after seeing exactly what was needed and nothing more. Use it for snap judgments — one metric, one screenshot, one line of a proposal and the verdict is already in.

templates.name: I Serve the Soviet Union

templates.name: Kronk "No No, He's Got a Point"

templates.name: Lisa Simpson "I'm a Sign, Not a Cop"

templates.name: Pathetic Cat

templates.name: Spongebob Inhalar Chamaco

templates.name: Shocked Baby

When the client asks to see last quarter's numbers

templates.name: Kitten and Mountain of Food

templates.name: Bee Movie Shocked
